title: Statistic (3) of P-L4-013 measured on the public pages: labels recur in their own page's text barely more than in another page of the section, and no more strongly than ordinary words do, so it would not separate language from a page-local meaningless procedure
statement: The third statistic proposed in P-L4-013 (a label word recurs in its own page's running text more than in other pages') needs no picture annotation, so I measured it now on the public practice pages only (226 pages; nothing from the hidden pages). Selection: the 46 public pages with at least three label words and at least thirty words of other text (15 pharmaceutical, 12 zodiac, 10 biological, 5 astronomical, 3 cosmological, 1 text), 886 label words of three or more glyphs with no uncertain reading. Statistic: the share of label words that occur somewhere in the non-label text of their own page. Null: the same share after the label sets are dealt to other pages of the same section, 999 deals. Result, exact word: 0.096 on the own page against a null mean of 0.085 (95th percentile 0.097), p = 0.079. Allowing one glyph of difference: 0.366 against 0.335 (95th percentile 0.361), p = 0.030 on 199 deals. By section, exact word, no section is significant on its own: astronomical 0.036 against 0.042, biological 0.200 against 0.190, cosmological 0.174 against 0.108, pharmaceutical 0.068 against 0.066, zodiac 0.091 against 0.074 (p from 0.11 to 0.75). So there is at most a weak page effect for labels, a ratio of about 1.13 to 1. The comparison that matters: ordinary words show a page effect at least as strong as labels do. Holding out the last paragraph line of every public page with six or more paragraph lines (925 words), 0.351 of its words occur in the rest of their own page, against 0.267 in the rest of another page of the same section, a ratio of about 1.32 to 1. Matched for frequency (five bins of how often a word occurs in the public running text, ordinary words reweighted to the labels' mix; the other-page rate here is the average over all other pages of the section, so the label figures differ slightly from the deal above), the ratios are 1.21 for labels (0.096 against 0.080) and 1.35 for ordinary words (0.144 against 0.107). Bin by bin the picture is mixed: among fairly common words (11 to 40 occurrences) labels have the higher ratio, 0.198 against 0.110 where ordinary words have 0.199 against 0.134; among the commonest (over 40) labels show almost none, 0.378 against 0.367 where ordinary words have 0.681 against 0.512. Half of the label words (448 of 886) occur at most once anywhere in the public running text and so can hardly recur on their page at all. This is the page-vocabulary effect already on the record (F-009), and meaningless procedures with a local memory reproduce it. Consequence for P-L4-013: statistic (3) as worded measures page vocabulary, not reference. A procedure that writes labels with the same memory it uses for the text would pass it at least as well as the manuscript does, and the manuscript's own labels pass it only marginally. It should not be registered as a fact meant to separate language from meaningless text unless it is redefined against that baseline, for example as the excess of the label recurrence ratio over the ratio for ordinary words of the same length and frequency on the same pages, where on the public pages the manuscript's labels do not rise above ordinary words. Statistics (1) and (2) are not touched by this; they need agreed annotations, which do not exist yet. Limits: one transliteration (ZL), public pages only, the frequency match is coarse (five bins) and does not match word length, the bin-by-bin counts are small (65 to 448 labels per bin), and the section deal keeps page sizes with the text, not with the labels. Addendum: a first look at statistic (2), with object kinds that need no annotation. The transliteration's own locus types separate labels written on a container from labels beside a detached plant part, and twelve public pharmaceutical pages carry both (36 container labels, 141 plant-part labels, labels with an uncertain reading left out). If labels named their objects, labels of the two kinds might differ in form on the same page. Eight features of form were compared, each against the two tags shuffled within the page (2000 shuffles, two-sided): glyphs per label 6.9 against 6.1 (p = 0.07), words per label 1.00 against 1.09 (p = 0.10), first glyph o 0.53 against 0.57 (p = 0.70), opening ok or ot 0.39 against 0.37 (p = 0.84), final y 0.50 against 0.44 (p = 0.59), final l or r 0.08 against 0.23 (p = 0.05), a pedestalled gallows 0.03 against 0.03 (p = 1.0), first glyph d or s 0.14 against 0.19 (p = 0.44). The smallest of eight p values is 0.05, which is what eight unrelated comparisons give by chance about one time in three; nothing here survives the number of comparisons. So on the public pages a label's form does not tell a jar from a root. That is a null on a small sample (36 container labels), chosen features and one transliteration, not evidence of no meaning: names of containers and of plants need not differ in their first or last glyph. It does mean statistic (2) should be registered with the features fixed in advance and with the expectation, on this evidence, that it may well fail for the manuscript itself. Second addendum, the nearest thing the transliteration alone offers to the proposal's 'labels share roots with the text about the same object'. On the pharmaceutical pages each row opens with a jar and is followed by the plant parts drawn beside it; if a jar's label named a preparation and the parts' labels its ingredients, or the reverse, a jar's label might resemble the labels of its own row more than those of another row. Nine public pages have two or more such rows with clean readings (28 rows, 130 plant-part labels). Similarity is one minus edit distance over the longer length; null: the jars' labels dealt among the rows of their own page (3000 deals). Jar against all labels of its row: 0.244 against 0.253 under the null (p = 0.72). Jar against the first object of its row, the one drawn next to it: 0.263 against 0.257 (p = 0.39). No sign that a jar's label is related in form to the labels beside it. Together with the label-recurrence and jar-against-root results above, three text-only versions of the picture-text predictions come out null on the public pages. That is what a meaningless procedure would give; it is also what a language would give if labels are unrelated names, so these nulls do not discriminate either, and the proposal's statistics need a planted positive control (an invented-language page where labels do share roots) to show they could detect the effect at these sample sizes before a null on the manuscript is read as evidence. Third addendum: the planted control for the jar-and-row test, run on the same nine pages. I rewrote a share of each row's plant-part labels so that they begin with the first glyphs of their own jar's label, left everything else as it is, and reran the test forty times per setting (300 deals each, detection at p of 0.05 or less). Sharing the first two glyphs: a share of 0.1 is detected in 0 of 40 runs, 0.2 in 4, 0.3 in 22, 0.5 in 40. Sharing the first three glyphs: 0.1 in 2 of 40, 0.2 in 24, 0.3 in 39. So the null above rules out a strong convention (half the row sharing a two-glyph root with the jar, or a third sharing a three-glyph root) and is silent on anything weaker: a language in which one label in five shared a short root with its jar would usually pass unnoticed on these nine pages. The hidden pages are fewer still, so a registered fact of this kind would have less power than this; it should be stated with its planted detection rates beside it. Fourth addendum: the planted control for the first measurement in this note (a label recurs in its own page's text), on the same 46 pages and 886 labels. I replaced a share of the labels with a word drawn from their own page's text among the words occurring there at most twice, and reran the test forty times per setting (200 deals each). A share of 0.02 raises the own-page rate from 0.096 to 0.114 and is detected in 40 of 40 runs; 0.05, 0.10 and 0.20 likewise in 40 of 40. Unlike the jar-and-row test, this one is sensitive: if even one label in fifty were a page-specific word of the text around it, beyond what the manuscript already shows, the test would see it. The manuscript's own excess is about one label in a hundred (0.096 against 0.085, p = 0.08). So on the public pages the labels are, almost without exception, not the distinctive words of the text on their page: either the text does not name the labelled objects with the label's word, or it names them with common words, or the labels and text are unrelated. This is the most informative of the nulls in this note, and it bears on the reading of labels as plant or star names that the paragraph beside them then discusses. It remains one transliteration, exact-word matching, and exact-word matching only. I then ran the plant I had expected to be harder, labels replaced by a word drawn from their page's text in proportion to how often it occurs there, common words included: shares of 0.02, 0.05 and 0.10 are again each detected in 40 of 40 runs (own-page rate 0.112, 0.141, 0.188). So the test would also see labels taken from the common words of their page at one label in fifty; my expectation that this would be harder was wrong. Fifth addendum, removing the one-transliteration limit on the first measurement. The same test on the other pinned transliterations of the public pages: Takahashi 0.102 own page against 0.086 dealt (45 pages, 894 labels, p = 0.017); the RF transliteration 0.073 against 0.067 (45 pages, 759 labels, p = 0.225); Zandbergen-Landini on a fresh set of deals 0.096 against 0.085 (p = 0.071). So the three readings agree on a small positive excess, between half a label and a label and a half in a hundred, significant at 0.05 in one of the three and nowhere at 0.01. I had written above that the claim would fail if a second transliteration gave p below 0.01; it does not, but Takahashi comes closer than my summary of 'barely more than chance' allowed, and the fair statement is: a small excess that may be real, of a size (about one label in a hundred) that page vocabulary alone would explain, and far below what the planted controls show a naming relation of even one label in fifty would produce. By section in the three readings (own page against dealt, 1999 deals): no section reaches 0.05 in any reading. The zodiac pages are the most consistent (0.091 against 0.074, 0.100 against 0.079, 0.065 against 0.054; p = 0.11, 0.06, 0.23), and that is where labels and the ring text share a page most closely; the pharmaceutical pages, where labels would most naturally be ingredient names taken up in the recipe text, show nothing (0.068 against 0.067, 0.075 against 0.071, 0.044 against 0.050), and the astronomical pages nothing or less. Last addendum, the jar-and-row test on the other two pinned transliterations of the public pages: Takahashi 0.262 for a jar against its own row and 0.250 dealt (8 pages, 25 rows, 111 labels, p = 0.24); the RF reading 0.227 against 0.245 (7 pages, 20 rows, 79 labels, p = 0.89); Zandbergen-Landini on fresh deals 0.244 against 0.253 (p = 0.72). The sign of the difference is not even consistent between readings, so the null holds in all three. And the jar-against-plant-part comparison of label form on the other two readings, which qualifies what I wrote above about that test. Two of its differences recur in all three transliterations with the same sign and about the same size: labels written on jars are longer (6.9 against 6.1 glyphs in Zandbergen-Landini, 6.8 against 6.1 in Takahashi, 6.8 against 6.2 in RF; p = 0.07, 0.10, 0.18) and seldom end in l or r (0.08 against 0.23, 0.09 against 0.24, 0.07 against 0.23; p = 0.06, 0.09, 0.09). The three readings are of the same ink, so they are not three independent tests and their p values must not be combined; what the agreement shows is that the difference is not a transcriber's artefact. It is still a difference found by looking at eight features on a few dozen jar labels, and none of the p values passes 0.05. I therefore withdraw 'a label's form does not tell a jar from a root' as too strong: the fair statement is that jar labels may be somewhat longer and may avoid a final l or r, and that this is exactly the kind of claim that should be frozen now, as two one-sided predictions with these two features and no others, and scored once on the hidden pages. If it held there it would be the first picture-linked regularity in the labels on this record; I make no claim that it will.
check: On the public pages: for every page with at least three label words and thirty other words, the share of label words (three or more glyphs, certain) found in the page's own non-label text, against label sets dealt among pages of the same section; then the same own-page against other-page comparison for a held-out paragraph line. The claim fails if the label ratio clearly exceeds the ordinary-word ratio once words are matched for length and frequency more finely than five bins, or if a second transliteration gives a label effect at p below 0.01.
